author: Great Lakes Wire
title: Michigan prepares for rare multi-candidate Democratic Senate primary as contenders emerge
text:
Brian Calley President and Chief Executive Officer at Small Business Association of Michigan | Official website
Brian Calley President and Chief Executive Officer at Small Business Association of Michigan | Official website
Michigan Democrats are preparing for a rare, competitive U.S. Senate primary in 2026, marking the first time in over three decades that more than one major candidate is expected to compete for the party’s nomination. The anticipated candidates—U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), and Abdul El-Sayed—must each secure 15,000 valid signatures to appear on the ballot.
While such primaries have become uncommon for Michigan Democrats in recent years, they are not unprecedented. Since 1910, when Michigan began holding partisan primaries for the U.S. Senate, voters have participated in 39 such contests. Of these, only 14 involved Democratic primaries; in most cases, Democrats put forward a single candidate while Republicans had contested races more frequently.
Throughout this period, Democrats have presented 70 candidates for the U.S. Senate but have rarely challenged sitting senators within their own party. The only exception occurred in 1952 when Blair Moody faced a nominal challenge after being appointed to fill a vacancy but lost his re-election bid later that year.
The upcoming primary featuring Stevens, McMorrow, and El-Sayed could be highly competitive but must contend with several historical races noted for their intensity:
In 1994, following Sen. Don Riegle’s decision not to seek re-election, six prominent Democrats entered the race—including Carl Marlinga and Joel Ferguson—with Bob Carr narrowly defeating Lana Pollack by less than one percentage point.
The 1936 primary saw Prentiss Brown win by about two points over Louis B. Ward during a period of Democratic resurgence tied to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s popularity.
In 1976, Don Riegle won a four-way contest after Secretary of State Richard Austin was hurt by controversy over political contributions from branch office managers.
Other notable contests include Frank Picard’s victory in a crowded 1934 field and Carl Levin’s rise in 1978 when he defeated five other candidates before becoming Michigan’s longest-serving senator.
